key_insight: Many state-of-the-art Video-LLMs are 'directionally motion blind'—they cannot reliably tell basic signed image-plane motion (left/right/up/down); above‑chance answers often reflect prediction biases, not real motion understanding.
problem_solved: Diagnoses and localizes a fundamental failure mode in Video-LLMs—directional motion blindness—then evaluates and proposes practical ways to measure and mitigate it so models truly perceive motion rather than exploit spurious cues.
method: Design a controlled benchmark of simple single-object videos moving in cardinal directions to isolate signed image-plane motion.
Evaluate diverse Video-LLMs, quantify performance vs. chance, and analyze error patterns and prediction biases (e.g., confusion matrices).

Trace motion signals inside model processing to localize the failure and test mitigation strategies (e.g., motion-aware finetuning, data augmentations, optical-flow or frame-differencing inputs, and prompt/response calibration).
impact: Exposes a low-level perceptual blind spot that undermines temporal reasoning in Video-LLMs; fixing it improves reliability for downstream video tasks, evaluation rigor, and safety-critical applications that depend on accurate motion perception.
visual_elements: 4-panel demo: simple synthetic clips of a single object moving left/right/up/down (clear, labeled arrows).
Bar chart or violin plot showing model accuracies near chance and variance across models.
Confusion matrices highlighting directional biases (e.g., frequent mispredictions toward one direction).
Before/after comparison: attention/flow overlays or accuracy gains after applying mitigation (e.g., optical-flow input or finetuning).
paper_title: Which Way Did It Move? Diagnosing and Overcoming Directional Motion Blindness in Video-LLMs
paper_authors: Jongseo Lee, Hyuntak Lee, Sunghun Kim, Sooa Kim, Jihoon Chung
